title: Christopher Columbus
subtitle: The voyage that joined two worlds, and what it cost

package.intro: Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic four times and opened the Americas to European colonisation. For the Taíno people who met him, it was the beginning of a catastrophe. This documentary tells both stories: the navigator, and the governor sent home in chains.
facts: Born in Genoa in 1451, the son of a wool weaver
Sailed from Palos, Spain, on 3 August 1492 with three ships and about 90 men
Made landfall on 12 October 1492 on an island in the Bahamas its people called Guanahani
Made four voyages to the Americas between 1492 and 1504
In 1500 royal investigator Francisco de Bobadilla arrested him and sent him to Spain in chains
Bobadilla's report was rediscovered in the archive at Simancas, Spain, and published in 2006
Died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506
Columbus Day became a US national holiday in 1937; in 2021 a US president first proclaimed Indigenous Peoples' Day
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Library of Congress, Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Samuel Eliot Morison's Admiral of the Ocean Sea, Felipe Fernández-Armesto's Columbus, Bartolomé de las Casas's History of the Indies.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: COLUMBUS
lines.sub: The voyage that joined two worlds, and what it cost

lines: At about two in the morning on the twelfth of October 1492, a lookout on a small Spanish ship saw a pale shape in the moonlight. It was land: an island in what is now the Bahamas.
The man in command, Christopher Columbus, believed he had reached the edge of Asia. He went to his grave insisting he had.
Over the next twelve years he crossed the Atlantic four times, and opened the Americas to permanent European conquest and settlement.

lines.text: Explorer, or the start of a catastrophe?

lines: For centuries he was celebrated as a hero. Today, many see him as the man who began the destruction of the Americas' first peoples. Both views start from the same facts.

sections.name: A sailor from Genoa
lines: Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa, in northern Italy, in 1451, the son of a wool weaver. He went to sea as a young man.
In 1476 he survived a sea battle off Portugal, reportedly swimming ashore. He settled in Lisbon, the centre of Atlantic exploration, and sailed as far as West Africa.

lines.name: Christopher Columbus
lines.role: Genoese sailor who believed Asia could be reached by sailing west.

lines: He became obsessed with one idea: that Asia could be reached by sailing west, straight across the open ocean.

lines.text: Educated Europeans knew the Earth was round.

lines: A popular myth says people feared he would sail off the edge of a flat Earth. In fact, educated Europeans knew the world was round. The argument was about its size.

lines.label: Canary Islands to Japan, sailing west

lines: Columbus badly underestimated it. He reckoned Japan lay about four and a half thousand kilometres west of the Canary Islands. The real distance is more than four times that.
Portugal's experts rejected his plan, correctly, as bad arithmetic. Had the Americas not been in the way, his crews would almost certainly have died at sea.

sections.name: The voyage

lines.name: Queen Isabella I
lines.role: Queen of Castile. With Ferdinand of Aragon, she backed the voyage.

lines: He spent years seeking backers. In 1492, Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand of Aragon agreed to fund him, just months after their armies had conquered Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.

lines.title: Capitulations of Santa Fe
lines: A tenth of the wealth found
His terms were enormous: the title of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, the government of any lands he found, and a tenth of their wealth.
On the third of August 1492, he sailed from Palos in southern Spain with three ships, the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María, and about ninety men.
After repairs in the Canary Islands, they left on the sixth of September and sailed west for five weeks. As the days passed with no land, the crews came close to mutiny.

sections.name: Landfall
lines: They landed on an island its people called Guanahani. Columbus claimed it for Spain and renamed it San Salvador. Exactly which island it was is still debated.
Its people were Lucayans, part of the Taíno peoples whose farming and fishing villages stretched across the Caribbean. They met the strangers with curiosity and gifts.

lines.text: They would make good servants. With fifty men, they could all be subjugated.

lines: In his log, which survives in a summary made by a later friar, Columbus noted that they had no iron weapons. He wrote that they would make good servants, and that with fifty men he could subjugate them all.

lines.place: Hispaniola · the Santa María runs aground

lines: He sailed on to Cuba and to an island he named La Española, Hispaniola. On Christmas Day the Santa María ran aground. He left thirty-nine men behind in a small fort and sailed home.
In Spain he was received in triumph, with gold ornaments, parrots, and a handful of Taíno people he had taken with him.

sections.name: Governor
lines: His second voyage, in 1493, was a fleet of seventeen ships and well over a thousand men, sent to found a colony.
At Hispaniola he found the fort burned and all thirty-nine men dead. They had raided local villages, and had been killed in return.

lines.name: Admiral Columbus
lines.role: Viceroy and governor of the Indies, 1493 – 1500.

lines: Columbus now ruled the colony as governor. He was a gifted navigator but a poor administrator, and the colony was soon short of food and full of resentful settlers.
In 1495 he shipped about five hundred Taíno captives to Spain to be sold as slaves. Around two hundred died on the voyage.
That same year, his forces, with horses and attack dogs, crushed a Taíno uprising.

lines.title: The gold tribute
lines: Or cotton where there was none

Desperate to show a profit, he imposed a tribute. Every Taíno aged fourteen or over had to deliver a set amount of gold every three months, or cotton where there was no gold. Those who failed were severely punished.

Forced labour, violence, hunger and, above all, new diseases did the rest. Estimates of Hispaniola's population before 1492 range from about a hundred thousand to several million. Spanish counts a generation later found only tens of thousands left.

sections.name: In chains
lines: Complaints reached Spain from priests and settlers alike. In 1500 the monarchs sent a royal investigator, Francisco de Bobadilla, to Hispaniola.
Bobadilla heard testimony that Columbus and his brothers had ruled brutally, including over Spanish colonists. He arrested all three and shipped them back to Spain in chains.
Bobadilla's report was rediscovered in a Spanish archive and published in 2006. Its witnesses describe severe punishments, even for colonists who complained.
The king and queen freed Columbus and restored his wealth, but they never let him govern again.

sections.name: Last voyages
lines: He made two more voyages, reaching the coast of South America in 1498 and Central America in 1502. On the last, his worm-eaten ships left him stranded on Jamaica for a year.
When local people stopped bringing food, he used an almanac to predict a lunar eclipse and told them it was a sign of God's anger. The food started arriving again.
He died in Valladolid, in Spain, in May 1506, a wealthy man, still fighting the crown for the titles and income he believed he was owed.

sections.name: The case for and against

lines.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
lines.role: Colonist turned friar. Denounced Spanish cruelty to the Taíno.

lines: The case against Columbus began in his own century. Bartolomé de las Casas, a colonist who became a Dominican friar, condemned the treatment of the Taíno and preserved Columbus's own writings.
Critics point to the slaving, the forced tribute, the punishments, and the pattern of conquest that others followed across the Americas.

lines.text: Judge him as a man of the fifteenth century, and as a navigator.

lines: Defenders say he should be judged by the standards of his own time, that most deaths came from diseases nobody understood, and that his voyages were a feat of seamanship and nerve. Critics reply that even his own monarchs found his rule too harsh.

lines.text: He was not the first. He was the one that lasted.

lines: He was not the first European to reach the Americas. Norse sailors had landed in Newfoundland around the year 1000. But his voyages were the ones that lasted.

sections.name: Legacy

lines.head: The Columbian Exchange
items: Horses and wheat to the Americas

lines: What followed is called the Columbian Exchange. Potatoes and maize fed Europe and Asia. Horses and wheat reached the Americas, and so did smallpox, measles and, within a generation, the transatlantic slave trade.
In the United States he became a national hero, especially to Italian Americans, who faced prejudice of their own. Columbus Day became a national holiday in 1937.
Indigenous groups and others have long challenged that celebration. In 2020, dozens of his statues were taken down. In 2021, a US president proclaimed Indigenous Peoples' Day for the first time.
Columbus was a bold navigator and a harsh, greedy governor. The arguments over him are really arguments about how to remember everything that began in 1492.
He did join two worlds. But the people who had lived in one of them for thousands of years paid the first and heaviest price, and any honest account has to begin there too.
